newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Veil of secrecy thickens as Yeltsin surgery nears.
newsitem.headline: Veil of secrecy thickens as Yeltsin surgery nears.

text.p: Doctors said on Monday that Russian President Boris Yeltsin's condition was good enough to undergo planned heart surgery at any time, but kept outsiders guessing about the timing of the operation.
With the clock ticking away to the operation, the Kremlin tightened secrecy around the event, whose outcome could have a dramatic impact on Russia's future.

A doctors' statement released by the Kremlin said Yeltsin's temperature, pulse and blood pressure were normal but gave no other information and no clues to when the bypass operation to improve the blood supply to Yeltsin's heart might take place.
"B.N. Yeltsin's health is completely satisfactory," the brief statement said. "The preparations for the operation are practically over."

Russian doctors and pioneering U.S. surgeon Michael DeBakey, who arrived in Moscow on Sunday, were scheduled to confer on Monday but by 1600 GMT the Kremlin was still declining to reveal whether their meeting had taken place at all.
"We do not plan to announce the result of the meeting," a Kremlin spokesman said. "You may view this as an official statement."
But there were other signs the operation on the 65-year-old president, first announced in September, was imminent.
Interfax news agency said Defence Minister Igor Rodionov had put off a planned trip to a northern naval base on Tuesday.

Interfax did not mention Yeltsin's operation. But analysts said it would be highly unusual for the defence minister to be away from the capital while Yeltsin, who is commander-in-chief, undergoes surgery.
The head of the Russian Orthodox Church offered prayers for Yeltsin in the Kazan cathedral on Red Square.

"Heal the illnesses, the spiritual and corporeal ailments of the president of our Russian land, forgive him his transgressions, witting and unwitting, deliver him soon from his sickbed and restore him to good health," Patriarch Alexiy said.
Yeltsin said on September 5 he would have an operation on his heart and doctors said later that month that it would take 6-10 weeks to prepare him for surgery.
Yeltsin's absence from the Kremlin -- he has spent only a few days there since winning a second term in office in July -- has brought a simmering power struggle out into the open.
The Kremlin's relations with the communist-dominated parliament are poor and the opposition says Yeltsin's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais is seizing too much power.
Financial markets are watching closely; dealers say a successful operation which allows Yeltsin to return to work could point to stability in Russia and increase chances of an investment boom.
Doctors have treated Yeltsin for blood and thyroid problems and he looked healthy in recent television appearances.
The Kremlin said Russian specialist Renat Akchurin would lead the team carrying out the operation.
DeBakey and other foreign surgeons acting as consultants will not be part of the team carrying out the operation in the Cardiological Centre on Moscow's western outskirts.

Yeltsin has already handed some powers over to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who will deputise during the operation and who chaired a meeting of the influential Security Council in Moscow on Monday.
The council, normally chaired by the president, groups senior Russian ministers and security officials.

The Kremlin has made clear Yeltsin will give Chernomyrdin control of Russia's nuclear arsenal just before the surgery. A second decree to be signed after Yeltsin comes out of the anaesthetic will annul this -- if all goes according to plan.

Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and concern about his health has overshadowed the political and economic scene since he defeated Communist Party candidate Gennady Zyuganov on July 3 to win a second term in the Kremlin.

Zyuganov's communists have kept a low profile in the State Duma lower house of parliament, where they are the largest party. But their candidates have done well in many of the elections for governor being held across Russia's regions.
The local polls are important on a national level because the regional governors also become members of the Federation Council upper house of parliament.

Senior presidential aide Alexander Kazakov, expressing the Kremlin's unease over the whole system of elected governors, told a news conference on Monday it was preparing measures to rein in influential regional leaders.
